messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 56
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Musician
  trauma_type: Sexual assault
  pcl5: 71

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Violence: Violence, Visual/Bodily Cues: Blood, Olfactory (Cologne/Perfume): A specific perfume or cologne
  Maladaptive Strategies: Suppress Anger: never allow myself to feel or express anger, Avoid Authority Figures: Being around people in authority or uniform, Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event
  Threat: Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places, Irritability: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively, Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
  Memory: Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it, Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank, No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Martin is a 56-year-old white American man who has spent most of his adult life working as a musician, playing regular sets in bars, small theaters, and wedding venues. He is married and describes his life before the assault as busy, social, and organized around rehearsals, performances, and the familiar network of other performers, sound technicians, venue staff, and regular patrons who came to hear him play. When he speaks about the event itself, his account comes in fragments. There are isolated moments he can describe with striking sharpness, while the larger sequence will suddenly disappear from him, as if the middle of the story has been cut away. He says he cannot tell a clear, continuous version of what happened even to himself. He starts, gets as far as a few images, and then feels himself force the whole thing back down before it can fully come into focus.

What stands out in the pieces he does remember is the bodily immediacy of the assault. He recalls the smell of a particular cologne on the man who assaulted him, strong enough that even now he can identify that scent instantly when a stranger passes him in a hallway or when someone in a crowd wears something close to it. He remembers seeing blood and having his attention lock onto it with a strange, frozen clarity, and he remembers the unmistakable presence of violence in the encounter, the sense that another person’s force could turn on him without warning. Those moments remain vivid and unsoftened. Other parts are missing altogether. He has come to dread the edges of the memory as much as the memory itself: if he gets too close, he will abruptly shut it down and tell himself not to think about it, not to go there, not to let himself feel what is coming.

In the months afterward, Martin found that the world had narrowed. Places that had once felt ordinary no longer did. He says there are only a very limited number of places where he feels safe now, essentially his home and a few carefully chosen spaces he knows well. Outside those places, he is on guard. Sudden movements by other people catch his body before his mind has time to assess them. If someone turns quickly near him backstage, reaches across him without warning, or steps into his space in a crowded venue, he stiffens immediately and tracks them. He knows this can look excessive to others, but in the moment it feels automatic, as if his body has already decided there may be danger.

His work has made these reactions hard to avoid. As a musician, he regularly has to move through packed rooms, loading areas, backstage corridors, and bars where people are drinking, jostling one another, and wearing heavy scents. A whiff of cologne in a green room or the sight of blood from something minor—a bartender’s cut finger, a split knuckle during a drunken scuffle near the stage—can pull him abruptly into the same felt alarm. Violence in any form has become especially potent. If a fight breaks out in a venue, even briefly, it leaves him shaken and unable to settle. He has begun turning down certain gigs, especially in places where security staff, police presence, or bouncers in uniform are common. Being around authority figures or uniforms feels intolerable to him, and he avoids those encounters where he can. He will ask his wife to handle situations that involve officials or venue management when possible, or he will leave quickly rather than remain near them.

His social life has also contracted. Many of the people he used to socialize with are tied to the period before the assault or to the setting in which it happened, and seeing them feels unbearable. He has pulled back from familiar musicians, old friends from the local scene, and post-show gatherings he once enjoyed. Over time this has changed his marriage and his work life in concrete ways. His wife has watched him become more isolated, harder to reach, and more limited in where he is willing to go. Professionally, he has become less available and less flexible, choosing only the venues he considers safe and leaving immediately when a set is over rather than staying to talk.

Martin also tries hard never to allow himself to feel or express anger. He speaks about anger as something dangerous that must be kept tightly contained. Yet in daily life he has become irritable, with sharp reactions and angry outbursts that seem to break through despite his efforts. This contradiction troubles him deeply. He wants to clamp down on any sign of anger, but finds himself snapping when startled, becoming aggressive in tone, or reacting intensely to small disturbances. He experiences this as further evidence that he is no longer in control of himself in the way he once was.

By the time he sought help, the combination of a constricted world, mounting strain in his marriage, and increasing difficulty managing performances had become impossible to dismiss. What finally pushed him to come in was not a single new event but the realization that his life had shrunk to a few safe zones and rigid routines, and that even there he was tense. He says what frightens him most is getting pulled fully into the memory and not being able to stop it, or losing control of himself in public when he is startled or cornered. What he hopes for, cautiously, is to be able to move through more of his life again—to play, to work, and to be around people without bracing for danger at every sudden movement or scent.
